_why: The device server this app carries inside itself.
ForgeFX is a separate project (MIT, sKuhLight) and we ship a copy of it in the
installer. Two consequences follow, and this file is both of them.
First, we vendor from our own private mirrors rather than from upstream. What
goes inside something we sign should not depend on another account's repository
still being there, still being public, and still having the history it had last
week. `upstream` records where each mirror came from, because provenance is the
thing a copy loses first.
Second, the pin is the commit. The mirrors carry every branch and the whole
history but no tags, so `tag` is a label for people and `commit` is what
scripts/vendor-forgefx.mjs actually asks GitHub for. That is stricter than
cloning a tag and checking it afterwards: there is no window in which the wrong
code is on disk. Where a remote does have the tag, the script still checks it
points here.
forgefx-midi is the preset codec ForgeFX depends on. Its ref is not ours to
choose: ForgeFX pins its own sibling in stack.lock.json for exactly the tag
builds we are copying, so the script cross-checks the tag below against that
file and refuses to build a pair upstream never released together.
The pin is a branch of the mirror rather than a plain upstream commit. Naming
the preset or a scene was refused by the host's own remoteAllowed() — absent
from the writes it permits and absent from the list of things it says are
never remotely reachable, which reads as an oversight rather than a boundary.
It is an edit-buffer write like every other one allowed there, and committing
to a slot is still refused, so it cannot overwrite anything on the unit.
Kept on a branch so the mirror's main stays a clean copy of upstream: the next
upstream release is a rebase of one commit rather than a merge conflict.
The branch now also carries host addressing. The remote channel is per
ACCOUNT, so a request is not sent to a host -- it is shouted, and every host
signed into that account answers it. With two Macs that meant a read was
answered twice and a WRITE WAS CARRIED OUT TWICE, on two different units. The
host now honours an optional `host` field naming the Mac a request is meant
for, and stays silent on anything addressed elsewhere. Absent on every request
from a client that has only ever seen one host, so it is inert until there are
two.
And tuner readings now cross the relay. They were dropped with the meter and
CPU cadence, which was right for those -- they run continuously for any
subscribed client -- and wrong for the tuner, whose poll exists only while
somebody has it open. Dropping it broke the one place a remote tuner is worth
anything: tuning from a phone away from the Mac. Throttled to one reading
every 80 ms so a future poll cadence cannot flood the relay.

The branch moved again, and for a fault a player hit twice: "PRESET_DUMP_HEADER: expected func 0x77 at offset 0, got 0x78" on switching presets. The server decided a preset dump had arrived by checking for chunks and a terminator and taking the header on trust, so a dump whose HEADER went missing was handed to the codec instead of being re-read by the retry that was already there. The fix sits on top of the three patches above rather than on upstream main, which does not carry them — re-pinning to main would have taken renaming, host addressing and the remote tuner away with it.

And the branch carries one more, for the units this app has no cable to. The capability report answered HOW MANY PRESETS a unit stores by reading the shape of its SIGNAL CHAIN -- grid meant 512, linear meant 104. Those are not the same fact. A VP4 runs a linear chain and is not an AM4, so it was served the AM4's 104 locations and its A01..Z04 bank letters; an Axe-Fx II, having a grid, was told it held 512 where the codec's own gen-2 device says 384. Every driver now states its own count, and a unit nobody has counted on hardware says null rather than borrowing another one's.

And two commits come back from the mirror's main, for a fault a player could hear: the audio cut out for as long as the app was open and stopped the moment it was closed. The Play screen asked for every block's monitors twice a second, which the host can only answer by fetching the whole grid -- and gen3.ts liveMonitors() already warned what that costs, a full ~24KB preset dump on every tick, serialised ahead of every other read on a port that takes one request at a time. The client half is fixed in the app; these are the server half. GRID_TTL_MS goes from 500 ms to 15 s so one dump serves more than one caller, and storedPresetName reads a slot's name over fn 0x0D without loading the preset at all -- which matters because the app walks all 512 slots four seconds after connecting, and until this every one of those names cost a dump. Both were written on main and neither had reached this branch, which is the whole hazard this file exists to record.

And the last of it, for the same fault. The telemetry supervisor starts on its FIRST event listener -- subscribe() calls startMeters() unconditionally -- and at the balanced default each 100ms tick is four back-to-back output-meter round trips, roughly forty SysEx transactions a second at the control processor of a unit that is also making sound. A phone opening the app supplies that listener through the relay bridge and closing it removes the last one, which is exactly the shape of what was reported: the sound cutting out while the app was open and settling the moment it was closed. Those meters draw one bar. POST /telemetry/meters lets a client say it is not drawing it, and the loop then keeps only the front-panel scene and channel watches -- a footswitch press still lands -- at 800ms instead of 100ms. Measured over the same 900ms window on ForgeFX's own suite: 35 frames against 2. Defaults on, so a client that has never heard of the route keeps its bars.

And the last two, for a phone. Verifying a write means clearing the parameter cache and reading the value back, and remoteAllowed() had no DELETE branch at all -- so from a phone the clear was refused, the read came out of a cache one write behind, and NOTHING a remote client wrote could be verified. A log from an iPhone showed five parameters in a row reported unverifiable, each reading back the value of the write before it; every one had landed. DELETE /device/cache is a read-side hint that stores no value, touches no preset and reaches no slot, which is why it sat outside the rule rather than inside the list of things never remotely reachable. GRID_TTL_MS going from 500ms to 15s made it matter more: a cache that lives thirty times longer needs the one client that cannot reach the machine to be able to drop it.

And the port is opened again once it has closed underneath the server. transport() shared one open across every caller through a promise that was only ever cleared when an open FAILED; a port that opened fine and then went away -- the unit off and on, the cable out and back, the Mac waking -- stayed resolved for good, and every request after it was handed the same dead port and answered `port not open` until the connection was picked again by hand. A player's log from a phone: every read, every scene tap and every preset select refused that way while the unit sat there switched on and the Mac called itself connected, because health() asks only whether the port is LISTED. The server now drops a transport that is no longer open and opens the port afresh for that request; the serial transport says in the Mac's log when its port closed and whether the device went away.

And the server says on /diag when its port was lost, why, and what it said. The desktop app starts it with stdio inherited, and an app opened from the Finder inherits nothing anyone can read, so every line about a port closing or a reopen went nowhere and from a phone all of it was `port not open`. The serial transport keeps when and why its port closed; the registry keeps the last ten reopens as `reopens`; the last eighty console lines ride /diag as `recent`, with the uptime. The phone's Copy log asks for it.

And an AM4 is taken over MIDI ahead of the serial node it also exposes. The first /diag report from a Mac said it all: `resolved: midi AM4`, no Fractal serial node listed, 59 of 59 writes verified, not one fault -- while every failure earlier that day carried the serial transport's own words. The AM4 shows up on a Mac both ways at times; resolveConn() took serial first because on the FM3 it is the fast link, and the AM4's serial node answers the fn-0x00 handshake and then loses the port on the first real read. midiFirstConn() picks MIDI for a unit named AM4/AM-4/VP4 before serial gets a look; a manual override still wins; an FM3 keeps serial.

And a placement or a rename on the AM4 is judged by reading it back. Over USB-MIDI the AM4's 18-byte command ack has not been seen once while every write lands (59 parameter writes "unit said ok:false", all read back as sent), so a block placed into an empty preset was reported refused with the block in the slot. placeCell() and setPresetName() treat the ack as a hint and the read as the answer. /diag keeps four hundred lines rather than eighty, because eighty is twelve seconds of an AM4's own polling.

The codec moves with it, and the +suffix on its ref says why. buildTree() in the gen-3 preset Huffman decoder recursed for ever on an empty or truncated bitstream -- BitReader answers 0 past the end of its buffer and a 0 bit means 'internal node, read two more subtrees' -- so every slot whose raw_patch header reports compSize 0 answered GET /presets/{n}/summary with "RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded". Six slots of one FM3 did exactly that. vendor-forgefx.mjs cross-checks ForgeFX's stack.lock.json against the tag below and refuses a pair upstream never released together, so both had to move together.

And a block read slices its channels by the unit's own item count. A phone reported knobs that "did not take" on blocks in channel B and D, reading back values that belonged to other parameters -- 255 for a crossfade time, 16000 for a delay time, factory defaults for three drive knobs -- while a knob on a block in channel A confirmed every time. The channel slice took its per-channel stride from the range-section table and never checked it against the bulk read's item count; when the two disagree, channel A starts at zero and reads right, and every other channel is offset. The unit's count now wins whenever the table does not divide it, each block read says its numbers on /diag, and an incomplete preset dump waits for the port to go quiet before asking again, because the re-request sent straight into the previous dump's tail collected the same stale terminator three times over.

And the Axe-Fx II, all three of it. Every gen-2 frame the codec built was addressed to the XL+'s model byte 0x07 and every reply it accepted had to carry it, so a Mark I/II (0x03) or an XL (0x06) -- which ignore frames meant for another model -- could not be driven at all, and the identify table called both unsupported. setAxeFxIIModel() now addresses the codec to one variant and the server keeps a driver per variant, each with its own preset count (384, 768, 768). And even an XL+ never finished connecting: GET /preset answered 501, because the gen-2 driver had no presetRef; it is now two small reads. Blocks placed on the grid landed one row down and one column right (placeCell shifted coordinates the route already takes from one), the model picker never appeared (the selector is effect_type on gen-2, not type), and an Axe-Fx II was offered the gen-3 rail screens. None of it has run on an Axe-Fx II yet. The commits sit on claude/axe-fx-ii in both mirrors, on top of the branches named below, which fast-forward to them when this ships.

And an AM4's scene names reach a phone. They live only inside a full preset dump, and the only route that dumped was POST /preset/backup, which the remote allowlist refuses by design -- so a phone showed names only for presets the computer's own window had happened to open: "Some of them work some of them don't." GET /presets/:n/scenes is the same stored-slot dump as a read that returns only the names, which the relay carries. A dump answering for another slot is refused rather than believed. On claude/am4-scene-names, on top of the branch below, which fast-forwards to it when this ships.

And the looper's buttons reach a phone. POST /preset/looper/control -- Record, Play, Stop, Dub, Undo, Once, Reverse, Half, the same write FM3-Edit's looper page sends -- was refused by remoteAllowed(), so a phone could see the Looper block and never press it. It is a performance control like a scene tap: it moves the looper's own audio, writes no parameter, stores nothing and reaches no slot. On claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd, one commit on top of claude/address-one-host, the branch every patch above lives on.

And a chain read that was already on its way when a block was placed is no longer kept. grid() cached whichever dump finished last; a placement cleared the cache, but a dump the Mac window had started a moment before finished afterwards and was cached as the current chain for fifteen seconds, with every new caller waiting on it too. A looper added from a phone came back missing from the gig screen until a preset change: "it saves it but doesn't register it immediately." Every write that changes the grid now bumps a generation and drops the in-flight read; a dump is kept only if nothing changed while it was being read. On claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd, on top of the looper commit.

And the AM4's tempo, which ForgeFX had no path for at all: GET /tempo answered 501, so a gig screen showed no tempo until TAP was pressed, and TAP never reached the unit. Fractal's family-wide tempo function (fn 0x14 GET/SET, 0x10 tap) is sent with the AM4's model byte on new opt-in routes, GET/POST /tempo/probe and POST /tempo/probe/tap. Additive only: GET/POST /tempo and caps.tempo are unchanged for every unit, so nothing that reads them sees a difference, and the probe is promoted once an AM4 is seen answering it. On claude/am4-tempo, one commit on top of claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd.

And the AM4's firmware, which /device reported as null, so a client showed 'fw —'. The AM4 answers the same fn 0x08 firmware query the gen-3 units do (the AM4 codec's describe.ts labels its reply from AM4-Edit captures). It is asked only after a real handshake detect; a forced AM4 profile still sends nothing. One more commit on claude/am4-tempo.

And the AM4's tempo, for real this time. Controllers -> Tempo turned out to be an ordinary parameter at (0x0002, 0x001C), found and read on Justin's AM4 with the app's AM4 check: its long read (0x0D) answers with the unit's own display, '250 BPM' at norm 1.0 and '107 BPM' at norm 0.36731, so the AM4's tempo runs 24..250. GET /tempo now long-reads it, POST /tempo writes SET_NORM and reads it back, POST /tempo/tap times taps on the server and sets the result, and caps.tempo is true for the AM4. One more commit on claude/am4-tempo.

And the AM4's own tuner screen. "On the AM4 the tuner doesn't activate on the device, it only shows it on the phone ... I know that it has MIDI support for activating and deactivating a tuner because I have a MIDI device that does it." The AM4 opens and closes its tuner on a MIDI Control Change, on whatever number the player chose under SETUP > MIDI/Remote > Tuner -- there is no factory number. POST /tuner on an AM4 now long-reads that setting (0x0001/0x0049) and the MIDI channel (0x0001/0x003A) with the same 18-byte read the tempo uses, and sends 127 on open and 0 on close on exactly the number and channel the unit names, over USB-MIDI only. NONE, or anything unclear, sends nothing and the readings go on as before; a close re-reads first and never sends its 0 on a number the AM4 no longer names, since that number may now be Output Volume. Never a SysEx write. The answer gains `screen`. On claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd, four commits on top of claude/am4-tempo, which this branch now carries.

And the relay host comes back by itself. A phone on another network got no answer for minutes while the computer app was open and signed in, and only a restart fixed it. realtime-js heals a dropped socket, a network change and a token that expired while asleep, but never a channel the Realtime server closed (phx_close: its own token-expiry timer, a failed re-authorisation of the hourly token push, rate limits). RemoteHost ignored every status after the first SUBSCRIBED and kept saying connected on that dead channel; a failed first subscribe also left a zombie that doubled the next 'req' handler. It now tracks the channel for its whole life, rebuilds a closed one with backoff (removeChannel for the topic, one set of handlers), retries a failed first join by itself, never runs a request from a superseded channel, and /remote/status says {enabled, connected, state, since, lastError, userId}. On claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd, one commit on top of the tuner commits.

And the meter loop starts quiet. "Stop the computer asking the unit for level readings nobody is looking at." (Justin, 15 October 2026.) The relay host subscribes to the registry from the moment the computer app signs in until it is turned off, for the scene and channel watches a phone needs to see a footswitch, and any listener started the meter loop with the output-level reads on -- so a signed-in FM3, FM9 or Axe-Fx III was asked for its four output levels about forty times a second the whole time the computer was online, phone or no phone. The meterGate commit above defaulted them on so that a client that had never heard of the route kept its bars; there was no such client. Nothing in this app has ever drawn those readings -- Play's signal bar is GET /preset/monitors/live, a direct read of the output block's own monitor -- and the relay host has never forwarded a meters or cpu event. So the default is off: the loop runs only the fn 0x13 channel and fn 0x0C scene watches, every 800 ms at balanced and 3.2 s at reduced, which is what a footswitch already had. An on is now a lease, an optional ttlMs held between a second and five minutes and a minute when absent, that lapses at the next tick unless it is said again, so a tab that said on and was closed, or an older Play that says on at every chain read, cannot keep the readings going; an off is immediate, the answer is still {ok, meters}, and /diag gains metersWanted. And a unit detected under a listener that is already there -- an FM3 put in place of an AM4 while the relay host is on -- starts the scene and channel watch again by itself; an older Play's ON used to do that by accident, and nothing says ON any more. The phone app and the website say off themselves at every connect and every two minutes (shared/relay-rules.mjs METERS_OFF_PATH), which is what quietens computers still on an older server, 1.87.4 among them. On claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd, three commits on top of the relay-host commit.

And a VP4's presets and scenes, by the plain MIDI a foot controller sends, as Fractal's own VP4 manual documents it. Nobody on the project has a VP4, and its SysEx scene and preset frames were seen once, as a written summary, beside the kind of frame that froze an AM4, so none of them is ever sent. A preset is one Program Change, PC 0..103 = A1..Z4, on the MIDI channel the player set (1 unless told otherwise), with no Bank Select and never sent again by itself; a scene is one Scene Select Control Change, value 0..3 = scenes 1..4, on the number the player set on the VP4 under SETUP > MIDI/Remote > Scene Select (1..119, not 32), which has no factory setting, so with no number nothing is sent and the answer says how to set one. Both go over the VP4's own USB-MIDI link only, never over serial, within 600 ms of reaching this computer or not at all, and each is checked by reading back the one structure record VP4-Edit itself polls: a preset up to three times, spread over a second, a scene once, and anything not seen to land is said in words, never as a failure. The same commits make that record the only thing a VP4 is ever asked for -- no Axe-Fx III grid request, no fn 0x1F poll of every block, no save, which wrote preset Y1 whatever slot was picked -- refuse an on/off or knob write to the settings blocks or to an effect the preset does not hold, refuse a Program Change to a phone or page that has not taken its update and sends no channel, and answer every refusal with a status and words, never 501 or 'unsupported'. /device says plainMidi for a VP4 alone, which is how the phone and the browser know this computer can; every other unit's answer is byte for byte what it was, and a GET /scene that fails on any other unit answers 500 as it always did. On claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd, nine commits on top of the quiet meters commits.

And an AM4's scene names survive a bad read. "The same names are not registering" (Justin, 21 October 2026, a Raspberry Pi 3 with an AM4): presets, the chain and the preset names read fine, every scene tile said 1-4, and Refresh names said Couldn't read them. Through a computer the only source of an AM4's scene names is the stored-slot dump behind GET /presets/:n/scenes, six messages and 12,352 bytes, and it was taken in one try: ended by the first 0x79 to arrive, a stale one included, cut off 200 ms after any frame, never asked again, outside the driver's reader lock. One short, merged or stale dump was a 503 and the names never came. A Pi 3 makes a bad attempt likelier: Linux takes MIDI in through the ALSA sequencer, whose per-client input pool holds about a third of one dump; a slow event loop can sit 200 ms in another callback mid-dump; and its USB controller is a weak one. Which of those it was is not known, so the read now survives all three: up to three attempts, each its own request on the transport and its own hold of the reader lock, so a tap queued meanwhile goes out between attempts; a wait that ends only on a terminator behind a header naming the slot asked for; the dump read from that header; an attempt that fails when the codec refuses it or it answers for another slot; a 1000 ms quiet window, which a good dump never waits out; and a wait for the line to go quiet before asking again. It stops sooner for a unit that has sent nothing to two requests, and for a read of another slot asked for since. Every failed attempt is kept in /diag with each frame's function and length, and on Linux the RtMidi client's ALSA input pool, so the next failure says which way it broke. POST /preset/backup with a slot gains the same read; one that hears only another slot now answers 503 in words where it used to save that other slot's bytes. Same request bytes as before, never anything new on the wire. On claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd, two commits on top of the VP4 commits.

And on Linux the unit's replies come in through ForgeFX's own ALSA sequencer client. "The same names are not showing up again at all. on the AM4" (Justin, 21 October 2026, a Raspberry Pi). On Linux RtMidi takes MIDI in through a sequencer client whose kernel input pool is 200 cells, about 4.6 KB of SysEx, less than two of the AM4's 3,082-byte dump chunks, and the kernel throws away what does not fit without telling anybody. Input is now read by a small python3 + libasound reader, started with `python3 -c`, whose pool is the biggest the kernel allows: 2000 cells, about 46 KB. Output, the AM4's Tuner Control Change included, stays on RtMidi. The reader gives way to RtMidi's input when python3 or the sequencer is missing, when it stops, or when it hears nothing on the first request, and FORGEFX_ALSA_SEQ_READER=0 turns it off. A Mac and Windows are unchanged. What it cannot fix is the cut before the pool: on a Pi 3 or 4, whose memory pages are 4 KB, snd-seq-midi's own buffer drops most of a dump first (the entry after next says it on /diag); on a Pi 5, whose 16 KB pages hold a whole dump, the pool is what could overflow, and this covers it. f0d5c8b, forgefx PR #13, from the session of Justin's other app.

And an AM4's loaded preset gives its scene names from the structure read. The fn 0x1F structure the edit watch already reads every few seconds, 192 bytes, carries the LOADED preset's four scene names at 0x30, 0x50, 0x70 and 0x90, 32 bytes each, right after its name: read off Justin's AM4 on 078 "Bad Wolf Rising LM". grid() answered scenes: [] on an AM4, so GET /preset/scenes had nothing, and the only road to the names was the 12,352-byte stored-slot dump that a Pi's MIDI input cut short. grid() now returns the four, unsaved renames included, so GET /preset/scenes and GET /preset/grid answer them on an AM4, the grid with the preset's name beside them, which is what ties them to the preset on screen. Stored slots (GET /presets/:n/scenes) still read their dump. Nothing new is ever sent to the unit: with the cache cold, either route costs the one structure read the chain, the edit watch and GET /preset already make, never a dump. 296a1ac, forgefx PR #14, from the same session.

And what Linux holds is said on /diag, a stranded fragment never eats the next reply, and an AM4 read the kernel cut is not asked again for nothing. On Justin's Raspberry Pi 3 every stored-preset read was "got 3095" of 12,352 bytes, and on 1.87.45 "got 3863": snd-seq-midi takes a USB-MIDI port's input into a buffer of input_buffer_size bytes, one 4 KB page there, and drops the rest, and RtMidi held the 768 bytes of chunk 2 that did get through and glued the next request's header onto them. /diag, on Linux over USB-MIDI only, gains linuxMidi: the page size, snd-seq-midi's input and output buffer sizes, the unit's input lines in /proc/asound (Rx bytes, Buffer size, Overruns) and RtMidi's input pool lines; nothing is added on a Mac, on Windows or over serial. The MIDI transport cuts a glued SysEx at each F0: a piece with no F7 is dropped and said once as a held /diag line, so the reply behind it reaches its request, and a message with no second F0 goes out exactly as before, on every unit. And the AM4's dump read stops after an attempt cut exactly the way a buffer that size cuts one (the header and as many whole chunks as fit, nothing after), where each retry lost the same bytes and held the reader about 3.8 s longer; its error keeps the codec's words first and adds the one-line fix, `options snd-seq-midi input_buffer_size=65536` in /etc/modprobe.d, which /diag keeps too. Every message, from RtMidi or from the own reader above, goes through the transport's one #receive. 5a2989e and 17a9f0d, merged with both commits above at f8be44e. On claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd, five commits on top of the AM4 dump retry commits.

And an AM4 amp's Out Boost, tapped from Play, goes out like a bypass. "On the AM4 the amp on off button should do an amp boost instead of turning the amp completely off" (Justin, 22 October 2026): Fractal Remote's amp pedal on an AM4 writes the amp's Out Boost, the codec's amp.out_boost (0x3a / 0x96, wire-verified from AM4-Edit's own toggle), with PUT /preset/blocks/58/params/150 {value: 0|1, continuous: false}. That route went through setParamValue, which waits up to 600 ms for the AM4's command ack, and over USB-MIDI that ack has never been seen, so every boost tap held the one MIDI queue for the whole 600 ms and a scene or preset tapped just after it went out up to 0.6 s late. setParam now sends the AM4's tap switches (AM4_TAP_SWITCHES: the amp's Out Boost and nothing else, exactly 0 or 1, the discrete write only) through setTapSwitch, the way setBypass, a scene and a preset go: queued with a 20 ms settle, the same 23 bytes setParamValue built (buildSetFloatParam, byte for byte buildSetParam('amp.out_boost', v)), the caches dropped as after any write, and {ok: true}. Every other parameter write, the normalised one for the same switch included, is unchanged. The phone and the browser send the same request to every computer. An older one sends the same frame at once too, but then holds its one MIDI queue up to 600 ms, so on a computer that has not taken this release a scene or a preset tapped within 0.6 s of a boost still goes out up to 0.6 s late (in 1.87.48 the amp's pedal was a bypass, which never held it). The boost itself works on every computer, so COMPUTER_NEEDED does not move. e2bfe70, on claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd, one commit on top of f8be44e.

And a copy of an AM4 preset that a write crossed is never kept (924ecfa). The server keeps the copy each dump of the preset makes for a moment (1.2 to 3.2 s by the cadence), so a page load reads the unit once; it kept the copy of a dump that a write landed in the middle of too. That dump began before the write, so it holds what the unit had before it, and every read asked after the write in that moment, one waiting behind the dump among them, was answered from it. On stage, through the amp pedal on an AM4 (its Out Boost): tap the solo scene, tap Boost while that scene's chain read is dumping, tap the next scene, and the next chain read and the boost read after it said the boost from before the tap, so the pedal read Boost off over a boosted amp until the scene after; a preset picked again during a scene's dump was read from the edited buffer's copy, and every block's on and off on the tiles had the same hole before the boost existed. Now every write, scene, preset select and channel moves a write generation, a dump notes it before it starts and keeps its copy only if it has not moved by the end; the caller whose dump it was still gets it, and a dump nothing crossed is kept exactly as before. It can cost the unit one more read, though: a read asked after a crossed dump finds no copy and makes its own dump, so on an AM4 a pedal tapped during a scene's chain read can cost one more whole-preset dump, for the boost read the app makes after that chain read. The app keeps that read (it is how a boost changed at the unit without an announcement, or a boost write that did not land, is put right at the next scene). The phone and the browser work with a computer without it, which can still answer from such a copy, as every computer before it did, so COMPUTER_NEEDED stays.

And an AM4 write by catalog key and the probe tempo drop the copy too (5b6e889). setParamByKey (PUT /device/params, and every block's channel through setChannel) and probeSetTempo (POST /tempo/probe) never called #invalidate(), the one thing every other write does: a read asked just after either was answered from the copy of the preset made before it, the write moved no write generation, so a dump it crossed was kept, and the edit watch was not told the write was the server's own, so it could announce it as an edit made at the unit. setChannel already dropped the copy after its write, so a channel is unchanged in effect, and neither the phone nor the browser sends the other two routes. The bytes written are the same; a read asked just after one now makes its own dump, as after every other write. COMPUTER_NEEDED stays. 5b6e889, on claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd, one commit on top of 924ecfa.

And the AM4's own tuner screen is kept up until the app's tuner is closed (ab7561e). "On the AM4 when turning on the tuner it stays on for about 15 seconds on the unit and then turns off. On the phone it stays on until you hit close. We want it to stay on until the user hits close." (Justin, 23 October 2026). Nothing sent to the unit is timed from the open: every message it gets in those 15 seconds also goes every 2 seconds or faster (the readings, the edit watch's reads), and the screen outlasts them; the AM4 manual names no tuner timeout. So the AM4 lets go of a tuner its Tuner CC opened, and the server now sends the open's 127 again every 3 seconds while the app's tuner is open (Am4Driver.keepTuner, AM4_TUNER_KEEP_MS): a screen the unit let go of is back within 3 seconds, one still up stays up. Safe only because the CC is a level, 127 opens and 0 closes: Fractal's way on the Axe-Fx III, the AM4 forum's own advice for this setting ("send the midi CC with the value 0 to turn off and 127 to turn on"), and his Close after the drop, whose 0 did not bring the tuner back as a toggle would have. No capture of the CC on an AM4 proves it. Each keep reads the Tuner setting again first, the same two long reads an open makes, and the 127 goes only when the unit still names the number it went out on (a number moved since may be Output Volume now), on the channel it names now; anything else sends nothing and forgets nothing. No 127 follows a Close: the registry counts a close from the moment it is asked for, before its turn comes, and the driver asks that before the reads, at the reader lock and just before the 127. Only the AM4 driver has keepTuner, so the FM3, Axe-Fx III, FM9 and VP4 are untouched; over a serial link, or on a new connection that opened nothing, nothing is sent. Bluetooth does the same on the phone (bleWire keepUnitTuner). The phone and the browser send nothing new and work with an older computer, whose AM4 tuner screen still drops after about 15 seconds, so COMPUTER_NEEDED stays. ab7561e, on claude/fractal-remote-continue-ljfqcd, one commit on top of 5b6e889.
